name: Colin Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Colin, thanks for your time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Burnside, a family sheep and wheat farm run by Alison Dunne and her son Rory. Most days I'm checking ewes, mending fences and moving the flock between paddocks, and in autumn I drive the tractor for drilling wheat, which I'm still slow at. I did twenty-six years with the post office before this, so I know every lane round here but not much about soil. The best bit is lambing at night, and the worst is my knees on the frozen hill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up farming at fifty-five?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The post office offered voluntary redundancy when they closed our sorting office, and I took the lump sum. Alison was short of hands, and she pays well because she can't keep young lads. My partner Ruth runs the children's section at the town library, and our two boys are grown, Ben's a teacher and Joe's a chef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it fizzles out, more or less. A bit like the self-scanning tills, handy but not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, to Rory, who's always on about drones. I'd post something in the local residents' group about not letting the hype distract the council from bus routes and the library. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on, which suits me. Sheep don't care about software. My only real worry would be the usual one, whether Alison sells up when she retires, but there are farms all round us that need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and getting better at the drilling, because I'm still the slowest on the tractor. I'd keep using the chatbot on my phone now and then, like when I asked it about foot rot last spring and then checked with the vet. I'd keep the redundancy money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Relieved, really, for Ruth more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Ruth more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because her job's the one with screens and bookings, and the council's always looking for cuts. If it fizzles, she's safe till she retires. My partner Ruth reads stories to toddlers on Tuesday mornings, and I'd hate for a council spreadsheet to decide a computer can do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Alison might sell up. What would you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd walk down the road to the Pattersons' dairy or the big arable place by the river. Farm hands are scarce here. I'd lose the sheep, which I'd be sad about, but not my wage.

say: I'd gently tell Rory the **drone hype** was overdone.
The council should focus on **buses and the library**, not chasing hype.
think: **Sheep** don't care about software, so my work carries on.
My only real worry is **Alison selling** when she retires.
do: Keep improving at **tractor drilling**, where I'm still slowest.
Keep using the **phone chatbot** occasionally and checking with the vet.
S0.quote: My partner Ruth reads stories to toddlers on Tuesday mornings, and I'd hate for a council spreadsheet to decide a computer can do that.
fieldNote: His worry points to **Ruth's library job**, the household's screen-facing income.
He uses AI **cautiously**, always checking with the vet afterwards.
Plenty of **nearby farm jobs** make the farm sale a small worry.

steps.text: Keep working at Burnside and get faster at tractor drilling
Keep using the phone chatbot for sheep questions, then check with the vet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to home. Ruth's library already uses a booking system that nobody likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say public jobs like libraries need protecting, and any savings from AI should go into services, not tax cuts. I'd say it at the residents' group and probably in a letter to the paper. I'd also say farm workers aren't exempt, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm all right for a good while, robots on a hill farm are years off. But Ruth answers questions, books rooms and orders books, and that's the list on the card. I think her hours could get trimmed, and we'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ruth and look at our budget with her on four days instead of five. Once Rory gets the new drilling app working, I'd learn it properly, since he says it plans the seed rate field by field. I'd keep the redundancy money untouched as our cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, but it'd be on my mind on the quad bike most mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the drilling app once Rory has it working. Why wait for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen enough gadgets break on the first day. I'll learn the drilling app the week after Rory (his boss's son) stops swearing at it, not the week before. That's always been my way, let the young ones find the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, but she'd go and volunteer at the school reading club the next day. Ruth isn't someone who sits still. We'd lose maybe a fifth of her pay, which hurts but doesn't sink us.

say: **Public jobs** like libraries need protecting from AI cuts, and farm work isn't exempt either.
AI savings should fund **services**, not tax cuts.
think: Robots on a **hill farm** are years away, so I'm fine for now.
Ruth's **library hours** could be trimmed, and we'd feel it.
do: Rework the **household budget** around Ruth on four days.
Learn the **drilling app** once Rory has it working.
feel: **Uneasy**, thinking about it on the **quad bike** each morning.
S1.quote: I'll learn the drilling app the week after Rory (his boss's son) stops swearing at it, not the week before.
fieldNote: His steady style shows in waiting for **proven tech** before learning it.
The household risk sits with **Ruth's thinking-heavy** library work.
A **fifth of Ruth's pay** is the loss he imagines, painful but survivable.

steps.text: Redo the household budget with Ruth on four library days
Learn Rory's drilling app once it works reliably
Write to the local paper about protecting library jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's 2028 for the thinking machines and 2031 for robots that could do my job. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it: a robot tax, a guaranteed income, and the government planning instead of hoping. I'd join whatever campaign the unions set up, even though I'm not in one at Burnside. I'd say it online, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means both our jobs go within three years. Ruth's in 2028, because a library computer that can talk to children and order books costs less than her. Mine around 2031, because Alison would buy a robot shepherd before she'd train another slow fifty-eight-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the redundancy money into a fixed savings account and stop the new car plans straight away. I'd join the farmworkers' union and the campaign for a robot tax. I'd talk to Ruth about her taking her pension at fifty-eight, and me stopping at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake, not because we'd starve, but because I'd have no idea what our sixties look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car, then the holiday to see Joe in the city. My old van has done two hundred thousand miles, and I'd make it do fifty thousand more before I'd spend on a new one. Small things, but it's how I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a strong cushion. Why lie awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the cushion was meant for retirement, not for five early years with no wage. And it's not just us, it's Ben's classroom and Joe's kitchen too. Everything I'd planned assumes there's work for people.

say: We need a **robot tax**, a guaranteed income and **real planning**.
I'd join a **union campaign** and speak up online for once.
think: **Both our jobs** go within three years: Ruth's first, then mine.
Alison would buy a **robot shepherd** before training a slow learner.
do: Move the **redundancy money** into fixed savings and cancel the new car.
Join the **farmworkers' union** and robot tax campaign.
Plan for Ruth's **early pension** and stopping myself at sixty-two.
S2.quote: My old van has done two hundred thousand miles, and I'd make it do fifty thousand more before I'd spend on a new one.
fieldNote: Two incomes ending **three years apart** is what turns him alarmed.
His **cushion** was built for retirement, not years without wages.
The progressive streak sharpens into **collective action** under pressure.

steps.text: Move the redundancy money into a fixed savings account
Cancel the new car and the city holiday to see Joe
Join the farmworkers' union and its robot tax campaign
Plan Ruth's pension at fifty-eight and stopping at sixty-two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, eight for the robots. 2034, so I'd be sixty-six. That's a different story for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them: retraining for library and office staff, and rules on how farms bring in robots. I'd say it at the residents' group and back candidates who take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd make it to sixty-five on the farm. Ruth would be the one caught, in 2031, at sixty-one. That's a few years short of her pension, which is a gap but one we could cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Burnside, since my job outlasts the warning. I'd put an extra two hundred a month into savings to cover Ruth's gap years. Once the robot salesmen start visiting farms, I'd try to learn how they work, so I'm useful if Alison buys one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a planning kind of anxious. I'd have a spreadsheet, which Ruth would laugh at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth do in those few years before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably move to the school library, where it's more about the children than the bookings. Or volunteer, if it came to it. My partner Ruth has spent thirty years getting kids to love books, and no machine can be that stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you feel about the robots on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. With five years, the robots would arrive after I'm gone, and I'd just be the old boy who taught the robot where the gate sticks. With two years, they'd be pushing me out.

say: Use the **few years** for retraining library and office staff.
Farms need **rules** on how robots are brought in.
think: I'll make it to **sixty-five** on the farm before the robots come.
Ruth gets caught in **2031**, a few years short of her pension.
do: Save an extra **two hundred a month** for Ruth's gap years.
Learn how **farm robots** work once salesmen start visiting.
S3.quote: My partner Ruth has spent thirty years getting kids to love books, and no machine can be that stubborn about it.
fieldNote: The **five-year warning** moves his own risk past retirement.
**Ruth's gap** before her pension is the main household threat.
He turns worry into **spreadsheets** and steady saving.

steps.text: Put an extra two hundred a month into savings for Ruth's gap
Learn how farm robots work once dealers start visiting nearby farms
Vote for candidates who back retraining for library and office staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking AI and 2039 for robots. I'd be seventy-one by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse, a decade is plenty to plan pensions, retraining and fair rules. I'd keep saying it to councillors and anyone in the queue at the post office. Old habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it barely touches anything, I'm retired before either part lands. Ruth too, just about, if she goes at sixty-six. It's the boys I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Burnside to sixty-five and enjoy it. I'd tell Ben and Joe to use the ten years well. Mostly I'd wait and see how the first few years go before changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my sons, calm for me and Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben and Joe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joe that cooking is hands-on, so he has the robot gap of three years extra. I'd tell Ben that a teacher who's good with teenagers will still matter. A decade's warning is a gift to my sons, as long as somebody in government bothers to open it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking across the three fast pictures, what's the main thing that changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the end comes before my sixty-fifth or after. On a hill farm the robots come last, so the question was never if, just whether I'd be sixty-three or seventy-one when they arrive.

say: A **decade** is plenty of time to plan pensions and fair rules.
I'd keep telling **councillors** and anyone in the post office queue.
think: Both parts land after **I've retired**, and Ruth just about makes it.
It's my sons, **Ben and Joe**, I'd be thinking about.
do: Encourage Ben and Joe to **use the ten years** well.
**Wait and see** how the early years go before changing plans.
S4.quote: A decade's warning is a gift to my sons, as long as somebody in government bothers to open it.
fieldNote: Ten years puts both household jobs **past retirement**, easing him.
He judges his sons by their **hands-on versus thinking** mix.
His frame is always **timing against retirement**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Keep working at Burnside until sixty-five
Watch the first few years before changing any savings plans
Talk with Ben and Joe about planning their careers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ruth and I would both lose our jobs within three years and years before our pensions. What would help is a bridging pension for people in their late fifties and sixties who get pushed out, and a robot tax to pay for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small family farms like Alison's. If only the big operators can afford the robots, the Burnsides of the world get bought out. That worries me nearly as much as my own job.

headlineQuote: On a hill farm the robots come last, so the question was never if, just whether I'd be sixty-three or seventy-one when they arrive.
portrait: A former **postal worker** who joined a family sheep and wheat farm after redundancy.
Progressive and **steady**, he learns new tools only once someone else proves them.
His household risk sits mostly with **Ruth's library job**, which is screen and booking work.
Alarmed in **AGI by 2028**, when both incomes end years before their pensions.
With five or ten years' warning, he retires **before the robots** and turns to his sons' futures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, ending both his and Ruth's jobs before their pensions start.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridging pension** for pushed-out workers in their late fifties and sixties.
A **robot tax** to pay for that bridging pension.
